relevant_findings.topic: Engineered wood substrate composition — OSB-core with zinc borate treatment
relevant_findings.finding: LP SmartSide is an engineered wood product composed of wood strands/fibers treated with the SmartGuard process (zinc borate for termite and fungal resistance) bonded with exterior-grade MDI resin and waxes. It is an OSB-core product — NOT cementitious like fiber cement. This means it is combustible, hygroscopic (absorbs moisture), and lighter weight (~1.5 lbs/SF vs 2.3 lbs/SF for fiber cement). Available in 16-foot lengths which reduces joints and speeds handling.

relevant_findings.topic: NOT alkaline — no alkali-resistant primer needed
relevant_findings.finding: Unlike fiber cement (pH 13.0 cementitious matrix), engineered wood is an organic wood-fiber product with neutral to slightly acidic pH. It does NOT require alkali-resistant primer. Standard 100% acrylic exterior primer is the correct field prime. This is a critical difference from fiber cement — saponification and alkaline burn are NOT failure modes for engineered wood.

relevant_findings.topic: Factory prime is transit protection only — field prime REQUIRED
relevant_findings.finding: LP SmartSide ships with factory primer applied. Like fiber cement, this factory primer is transit and weather protection only — NOT finish-ready. Field prime coat is REQUIRED before topcoat application for both performance and LP warranty compliance. Factory-primed products must be top-coated within 180 days or primer degradation occurs.

relevant_findings.topic: Edge sealing critical — moisture intrusion into OSB core causes irreversible swell
relevant_findings.finding: Edge sealing is the MOST CRITICAL maintenance requirement for engineered wood siding. Unlike fiber cement where cellulose capillary wicking is the mechanism, engineered wood's failure mode at cut edges is moisture compromising the MDI resin bonds, releasing internal stresses, and causing irreversible thickness swell ('springback'). Once the OSB core swells, it cannot be reversed. ALL field-cut edges must be sealed with end-cut sealer or field primer before installation.

relevant_findings.topic: Back-rolling is APPROPRIATE on engineered wood — especially textured profiles
relevant_findings.finding: Per Application Methods Doctrine, back-rolling is MANDATORY on T1-11 and rough-sawn siding profiles because deep vertical grooves need roller to distribute paint. This is a KEY DIFFERENCE from fiber cement where back-rolling is avoided. For smooth LP SmartSide lap, back-rolling is optional but recommended on textured/wood-grain profiles for optimal adhesion and uniform DFT.

LP SmartSide installs up to 22% faster than fiber cement due to lighter weight (~1.5 vs 2.3 lbs/SF), longer available lengths (16 ft — fewer joints), and compatibility with standard woodworking tools (no OSHA-mandated specialized tooling required). This translates to a handling speed advantage but does NOT directly affect coating production rates — spray/roll rates are determined by surface area and profile, not weight.

relevant_findings.topic: LP SmartSide warranty requires LP-approved paint systems
relevant_findings.finding: LP SmartSide warranty requires use of specific LP-approved paint systems with minimum 15-year warranty from the paint manufacturer. This is analogous to James Hardie's approved paint list but is a DIFFERENT list. Paint selection must be verified against LP warranty requirements before spec finalization. Two topcoats are required for warranty validity.

relevant_findings.topic: Surface texture factor for textured profiles
relevant_findings.finding: Deeply embossed textures (Cedarmill, roughsawn grain profiles) require a surface_factor of 1.15-1.30 vs smooth board for both material consumption (achieves correct DFT on textured profile) and production rate (additional spray passes or back-rolling needed). Same factor applies to engineered wood as fiber cement — texture geometry is independent of substrate material.

relevant_findings.topic: Siding profiles covered — lap, panel, T1-11
relevant_findings.finding: Three engineered wood siding profiles in scope: LP SmartSide lap siding (horizontal, most common), LP SmartSide panel (vertical flat panels — 4x8 or 4x9), and T1-11 (plywood-based panel with shiplap or channel groove pattern). T1-11 has distinct production characteristics — the vertical grooves require back-rolling and reduce spray efficiency. Lap siding is fastest, T1-11 is slowest due to groove complexity.

High-pressure power washing is PROHIBITED on engineered wood siding — strips paint films, damages surface texture, forces water behind wall assembly and into OSB core. Acid washing is also prohibited. Use low-pressure water spray (garden hose) with soft to medium bristle brush for cleaning. Same prohibition as fiber cement.

LP SmartSide ExpertFinish is LP's pre-finished siding system in curated colors. Like James Hardie ColorPlus, post-construction damage and caulking commonly compromise the factory finish. When field painting is required on ExpertFinish, treat as substrate state requiring bonding primer (factory baked finish is non-standard for field paint adhesion) before standard topcoat system.

relevant_findings.topic: Joint management — flashing preferred over caulk at butt joints
relevant_findings.finding: Manufacturers recommend joint flashing (slipsheets) behind field butt joints rather than relying on caulk. Caulk at butt joints frequently cracks under thermal and hygroscopic expansion stress. Flashing manages water effectively while allowing boards to move. Caulk is appropriate at siding-to-trim joints only. Do NOT caulk field butt joints on lap siding.

relevant_findings.topic: Moisture content protocol for engineered wood
relevant_findings.finding: Engineered wood siding must not be painted while saturated. Wood substrates must dry to MC < 15% before painting. Engineered wood is more moisture-sensitive at joints and cut ends than fiber cement. Moisture compromises the resin bond system and can cause irreversible dimensional change.

relevant_findings.topic: Spray tip selection for engineered wood siding
relevant_findings.finding: Lap siding (wood/fiber cement) uses 0.015-0.019" orifice spray tips, common tip codes 515, 517, 617. Acrylic latex is the typical material. 60-mesh (black) filter for latex paints. Same tip selection applies to engineered wood as fiber cement — spray atomization characteristics are determined by coating material, not substrate.

relevant_findings.topic: Application method dimension — spray_backroll is valid for engineered wood
relevant_findings.finding: Unlike fiber cement (spray only), engineered wood supports three application method values: spray (smooth profiles), spray_backroll (textured profiles and T1-11 — mandatory per doctrine), and brush_roll (fallback for small projects, occupied, high wind). The spray_backroll method requires a 2-person crew — one sprays, one follows with roller while coating is still wet.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives primer selection (field prime on factory-primed; standard acrylic primer on bare wood; bonding primer on factory-finished), prep sequence, and coat count.
condition_drivers.notes: SS_EXT_PRIMED_FACTORY is the dominant NC state for LP SmartSide. SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD occurs at cut edges, damaged areas, or T1-11 without factory prime. SS_EXT_PRIMED_FIELD means field prime already applied. SS_EXT_FACTORY_FINISHED covers ExpertFinish products damaged during construction. NOTE: SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT is NOT used — that is a fiber cement state. Engineered wood uses SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD for bare/damaged surfaces.

condition_drivers.impact: Production rate varies significantly. Lap: fastest (long horizontal runs, spray-friendly). Panel: moderate (large flat areas, fewer joints). T1-11: slowest (vertical grooves require mandatory back-rolling, reduced spray efficiency). Profile also affects application method constraints — T1-11 requires spray_backroll.
condition_drivers.notes: This is a configuration dimension, not a site condition.

condition_drivers.impact: Textured profiles require 15-30% more material (surface_factor 1.15-1.30) and slower production (back-rolling recommended). Smooth profiles spray at baseline rate without back-rolling requirement.
condition_drivers.notes: Surface_factor modifier on material quantity and production rate. Cedarmill is the most common LP SmartSide texture.

condition_drivers.impact: QT2: economy application, single coat acceptable on primed surfaces. QT3: standard 2-coat with clean cut-in. QT4: premium materials (LP-approved premium products), light sand between coats, raking light inspection. QT5 is not applicable to siding field — reserved for fine exterior millwork only.
condition_drivers.notes: Per Exterior_Substrates_Doctrine.md §5. QT5 excluded for siding field.

condition_drivers.impact: Spray is primary method for smooth LP SmartSide lap. Spray_backroll is MANDATORY for T1-11 and recommended for textured profiles (cedarmill, roughsawn). Brush_roll is fallback for small projects <750 SF, occupied adjacent areas, or high wind conditions.
condition_drivers.notes: KEY DIFFERENCE from fiber cement: spray_backroll is a valid and often required method for engineered wood. Fiber cement avoids back-rolling.

condition_drivers.impact: Height modifier on all tasks at elevation. ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50. Applied per elevation based on working height.
condition_drivers.notes: Treated as a HEIGHT MODIFIER (like FAC_HEIGHT for interior), not a site condition. A project may have ground access on one elevation and scaffold on another.

quality_differences.description: Economy exterior. Light clean, spot repair only. Single finish coat acceptable on factory-primed/field-primed surfaces. Economy-grade 100% acrylic exterior (must still meet LP 15-year warranty minimum). No edge precision required.

Standard residential. Full low-pressure wash. Field prime over factory prime (mandatory). Two finish coats with mid-grade LP-approved 100% acrylic. Clean cut-in at trim lines. Caulk all siding-to-trim joints. Back-roll textured profiles.
quality_differences.typical_use: Standard homeowner NC, most residential exterior engineered wood siding.

quality_differences.description: Premium exterior. Full wash with TSP. Field prime with premium primer. Two finish coats with premium LP-approved materials. Light sand between coats on visible areas. Raking light inspection before second coat. Crisp trim lines. Back-roll all profiles for maximum DFT uniformity.
quality_differences.typical_use: High-end residential, showcase homes, curb-appeal priority.

failure_modes.name: OSB core moisture swell (springback) at cut edges
failure_modes.description: The most critical failure mode for engineered wood. Moisture penetrating unsealed cut edges compromises the MDI resin bonds in the OSB core, releasing internal stresses and causing irreversible thickness swell ('springback'). Unlike fiber cement capillary wicking, this is a structural delamination of the core material that cannot be reversed once initiated.
failure_modes.prevention: Seal ALL field-cut edges with end-cut sealer or field primer BEFORE installation. Edge seal is non-negotiable for warranty and structural integrity.
failure_modes.detection: Swollen board edges at cut ends, delamination visible at edge, paint bubbling at joints, board thickness increase at termination points.

failure_modes.name: Joint failure from hygroscopic/thermal movement
failure_modes.description: Engineered wood is hygroscopic — it expands and contracts with moisture changes. Tight-butted siding without expansion gaps causes boards to buckle or cracks to form at inflexible caulk joints. Wood-based expansion coefficient is larger than fiber cement.
failure_modes.prevention: Ensure proper installation gaps per LP manufacturer specs. Use flexible paintable caulk at siding-to-trim joints only. Recommend joint flashing (slipsheets) behind field butt joints rather than caulk.
failure_modes.detection: Cracked caulk at joints, board buckling, gaps opening and closing seasonally, paint cracking at joint lines.

failure_modes.name: Factory primer degradation from extended exposure
failure_modes.description: Factory primer on LP SmartSide degrades if exposed beyond 180 days. Primer becomes chalky, loses adhesion, and no longer provides suitable base for field prime or topcoat. Exposure to UV and weather accelerates degradation.
failure_modes.prevention: Field-prime and paint within 180 days of installation. If exposure exceeds 180 days, assess factory primer adhesion with tape pull test. May require sanding and re-priming.
failure_modes.detection: Chalky primer surface, poor adhesion on tape pull test, discoloration of factory primer.

failure_modes.name: Moisture intrusion at T1-11 grooves and horizontal joints
failure_modes.description: T1-11 panel siding has vertical shiplap or channel grooves that collect and channel water. Horizontal joints where panels stack are particularly vulnerable to moisture penetration. Water standing in grooves accelerates coating failure and substrate degradation.
failure_modes.prevention: Ensure thorough coating in all grooves via back-rolling after spray. Verify Z-flashing at horizontal panel joints. Field prime must fully coat groove bottoms and walls.
failure_modes.detection: Paint failure concentrated at groove bottoms, substrate darkening at groove intersections, soft spots at horizontal panel joints.

failure_modes.name: Adhesion failure from painting over wet/saturated substrate
failure_modes.description: Painting engineered wood above 15% MC traps moisture behind the coating film. As moisture migrates outward through the coating, it creates blisters and lifts the paint film. Engineered wood retains moisture longer at joints and cut ends than solid wood.
failure_modes.prevention: Verify MC < 15% with moisture meter before painting. Do not paint saturated siding. Allow adequate drying time after rain events, particularly at joint locations and cut ends.
failure_modes.detection: Blistering paint film, peeling concentrated at joints and lower courses, moisture meter readings above 15% at affected areas.

notes_for_materials_manager: Engineered wood requires LP SmartSide-approved topcoat systems with minimum 15-year warranty from paint manufacturer. This is a DIFFERENT approved list than James Hardie. Verify paint selection against LP warranty requirements.

Field primer: 100% acrylic exterior primer for factory-primed surfaces (standard acrylic — NOT alkali-resistant). Engineered wood is NOT alkaline like fiber cement. Bonding primer for factory-finished (ExpertFinish) surfaces.

Coverage rate for engineered wood: 250-350 SF/gal per coat on smooth; apply surface_factor 1.15-1.30 for textured (Cedarmill/roughsawn). Same coverage as fiber cement — surface profile determines consumption, not substrate material.

Transfer efficiency: spray application has 50-70% transfer (25-33% more material than brush/roll). Spray_backroll uses spray material consumption rates (material is applied by spray; roller only redistributes).
Spray tip: 515 or 517 for lap siding, 517 for panel/T1-11. 60-mesh (black) filter for latex.
End-cut sealer is a separate consumable — needed for all field-cut edges. LP SmartSide Cut End Seal is the manufacturer-specific product.
Caulk: flexible paintable caulk (polyurethane or siliconized acrylic) for siding-to-trim joints only. Do NOT spec caulk for field butt joints.
ExpertFinish factory-finished products are IN SCOPE as SS_EXT_FACTORY_FINISHED — requires bonding primer before standard topcoat system.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Edge seal task is MANDATORY for SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD and SS_EXT_PRIMED_FACTORY (cut edges during installation). Include as conditional task in prep module.
Field prime is MANDATORY over factory prime (SS_EXT_PRIMED_FACTORY). Not optional. Include as required task in prime module.
Back-rolling is REQUIRED on T1-11 and roughsawn/cedarmill textured profiles. Optional on smooth LP SmartSide lap. This is the OPPOSITE of fiber cement (which avoids back-rolling).
Power washing PROHIBITED on engineered wood. Low-pressure wash only (garden hose + soft brush).
Module structure: setup -> protect -> clean -> prep -> prime -> apply -> cleanup -> teardown.
T1-11 profile requires specialized attention at vertical grooves — spray alone will not achieve DFT in groove bottoms. Back-roll is mandatory to force paint into grooves.
SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD does NOT trigger alkali-resistant primer (that is fiber cement only). Use standard 100% acrylic exterior primer.
SS_EXT_FACTORY_FINISHED triggers bonding primer path — ExpertFinish factory finish requires bonding primer for field paint adhesion. Light scuff sand entire surface before prime.
Caulking at siding-to-trim joints is a prep module task. Do NOT caulk field butt joints on lap siding (moisture trap).
Light sand between coats at QT4 only (not QT2 or QT3).
Moisture check: verify MC < 15% before painting. Engineered wood is more moisture-retentive at joints and cut ends than fiber cement.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Production rates vary by profile and application method. See production_rate_research section for detailed rates.
Lap spray: ~300-450 SF/hr (smooth), ~250-350 SF/hr (textured with back-roll). These rates are HIGHER than fiber cement lap spray (250-400) due to lighter weight and faster handling.
T1-11 spray+backroll: ~150-200 SF/hr (mandatory back-roll reduces effective rate significantly).
Panel spray: ~250-400 SF/hr (large flat area, fewer joints than lap).
Brush/roll rates: lap ~100-140 SF/hr, panel ~80-120 SF/hr, T1-11 ~60-90 SF/hr.
Access modifier (FAC_EXT_ACCESS): ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50.
Surface texture modifier: smooth=1.00, cedarmill/roughsawn=1.15-1.30 on BOTH material and production.
End seal task rate: ~60-80 EA/hr (brush sealant on cut ends).
Field prime rate: ~350-500 SF/hr spray on factory-primed engineered wood (slightly faster than fiber cement due to non-porous face).
Environmental conditions (wind, dew point, sun, temp) are EXCLUDED from estimation — they are SOP/process concerns, not estimatable at bid time.
Masking-to-spray ratio: 3:1 to 4:1 (masking hours to spray hours). Masking is a separate line item.
Coat system: 1 field prime + 2 finish coats standard at all QTs for NC. SS_EXT_PRIMED_FIELD skips prime.
QT2 may use single finish coat on field-primed surfaces — per Exterior_Substrates_Doctrine §4.5.

assumptions.value: New construction engineered wood siding field painting only (not trim, not soffit, not factory-finished ExpertFinish products in pristine condition)
assumptions.note: Trim around engineered wood siding is covered by separate exterior trim spec. Soffit covered by separate soffit spec.

assumptions.value: Required on T1-11 and textured profiles; optional on smooth LP SmartSide lap
assumptions.note: Explicit doctrine guidance: 'T-1-11 and rough-sawn siding: Deep vertical grooves need roller to distribute paint' — mandatory back-rolling. This is the OPPOSITE of fiber cement.

assumptions.value: QT5 not applicable to siding field applications
assumptions.note: QT5 reserved for fine exterior millwork, columns, decorative elements. Not siding field.

assumptions.value: Uses SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD for bare/damaged engineered wood, NOT SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT
assumptions.note: SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT is for fiber cement only. Engineered wood is wood-based and uses SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD. The Exterior_Substrates_Doctrine §2.3 incorrectly maps engineered wood to SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT — this is corrected in RC-001.

uncertainties.topic: LP SmartSide specific approved paint list
uncertainties.detail: Doctrine states LP SmartSide warranty requires 'LP-approved paint systems' and 'minimum 15-year warranty from paint manufacturer' but does not enumerate specific approved products. The approved product list must be verified against LP warranty documentation before materials.json finalization.
uncertainties.recommendation: Materials Manager should verify LP-approved products. SW Duration, SW Emerald, BM Aura are likely approved (similar to Hardie list) but require LP-specific confirmation.

uncertainties.detail: T1-11 spray+backroll rate (150-200 SF/hr) is extrapolated from doctrine guidance on rough-sawn siding with mandatory back-rolling (Exterior_Application_Methods_Doctrine Part A §5: 'Masonry/stucco spray + back-roll ~150-200 SF/hr'). T1-11 may be slightly different due to groove geometry vs stucco texture. No direct T1-11-specific rate in doctrine.
uncertainties.recommendation: Flag T1-11 rates for field calibration. Use stucco spray+backroll as conservative baseline.

uncertainties.detail: Doctrine identifies that ExpertFinish requires bonding primer but does not specify a product. The bonding primer must be compatible with both the cured factory finish (as substrate) and the field topcoat system.
uncertainties.recommendation: Materials Manager should specify a compatible bonding primer (e.g., SW Extreme Bond, Zinsser Bulls Eye 1-2-3 Plus) that adheres to cured baked finishes.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray or spray_backroll
zones.notes: LF-based — measured along house perimeter where landscape is adjacent. Brush/roll: drop cloth at base. Spray: full tarp width over plantings.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray or spray_backroll
zones.notes: Adjacent walkways. Brush/roll: drop cloth runners. Spray: full tarp coverage.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray or spray_backroll
zones.notes: Adjacent patio surfaces. Protection level driven by proximity and application method.
Exterior light fixtures mounted on or adjacent to siding. Bag or tape over fixture.
HVAC condenser units adjacent to siding. Full tarp cover during spray operations.

protection_zones_analysis.cross_spec_protection_note: Window and door protection during siding work is NOT this spec's responsibility. Window/door masking (glass, hardware, full unit cover) belongs in the respective window or door spec. If windows/doors are not being painted, their protection is scoped under the window/door spec or a separate protection mobilization. This prevents double-counting and ensures protection responsibility is clear per surface owner.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Soffit underside at eave. Often different color (white/light). Siding terminates at soffit/frieze junction. Separate scope.
Frieze board — horizontal trim board at the junction between siding and soffit/eave. Often a different (trim) color. Separate trim scope.
Corner boards frame siding field. Often different color (accent trim). Siding field terminates at corner board. Separate trim scope.
Window casing trim around openings. Siding terminates at casing. No cut-in — trim is a separate spec.
Door casing trim. Same as window casing relationship. Separate spec.
Foundation below siding. Not painted in siding scope. Drop cloth protection at grade level.

adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Identical adjacency pattern to fiber cement and wood siding — siding field has NO edge work requirements. All adjacent surfaces are separate specs (soffit, trim, foundation) or not in scope. Protection relationships only. Siding terminates at trim boards. Window/door protection owned by window/door specs.

affected_conditions.notes: Access type drives a HEIGHT MODIFIER on tasks, NOT a site condition. Applied per elevation based on working height. A project may have ground access on one elevation and scaffold on another.

excluded_conditions.rationale: Environmental conditions (wind, dew point, sun exposure, surface temperature) are important to the painting PROCESS but are NOT estimatable. They are unpredictable, change daily, and cannot be set as fixed conditions for an estimate. Including them adds estimation complexity with no practical benefit. They belong in SOP procedure notes and job-site decision protocols, not in production rate modifiers.

excluded.reason: Unpredictable. Changes hourly. Cannot set a fixed modifier for estimate.
Varies by time of day, sun angle, and season. Not predictable at bid time.
Weather-dependent. Not predictable at bid time.
Varies by elevation and season. Professional painters follow the shade — scheduling, not estimation.

valid_input_states.rationale: NC engineered wood siding arrives factory-primed (dominant state). Bare wood occurs at cut edges, damaged areas, or T1-11 products without factory prime. Field-primed means primer already applied — ready for topcoat. Factory-finished (ExpertFinish) is included because post-construction damage commonly requires field painting. NOTE: SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT is NOT valid for this spec — that is a fiber cement-specific state.

output_state.rationale: Output state is the painted finish. Satin is the most common exterior siding sheen. Actual output varies by sheen configuration (flat, satin, semi-gloss).

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: Protect finished trim from siding spray overspray. Unfinished trim needs no protection — it will be painted later.

Soffit is typically painted before siding (top-down sequencing). If already finished, light masking at the siding-soffit junction. Spray overspray drift is primarily downward/lateral — soffit is overhead and receives less direct exposure.
Foundation wall is rarely painted in NC context. Drop cloth at grade level is handled by landscape/hardscape protection zones, not adjacent surface protection.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Factory-primed LP SmartSide or equivalent engineered wood siding as delivered. Factory primer is transit/weather protection — NOT finish-ready.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Low-pressure wash (garden hose, NO pressure washer). Light sand for adhesion profile. Spot-prime any damaged/bare areas.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Field prime: 100% acrylic exterior primer over factory prime (standard acrylic — NOT alkali-resistant)
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Primary NC state. Field prime is MANDATORY for LP warranty compliance and adhesion performance. Must be top-coated within 180 days of installation or factory primer degrades. Unlike fiber cement, engineered wood is NOT alkaline — standard acrylic primer is correct.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Bare engineered wood — factory primer absent, damaged, or stripped. Cut edges exposed. OSB core visible at cuts.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Seal cut edges with LP SmartSide Cut End Seal or field primer. Clean. Light sand if rough.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Standard 100% acrylic exterior primer (NOT alkali-resistant — engineered wood is NOT cementitious)
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Occurs at field-cut edges and areas where factory primer is damaged, missing, or scraped during installation. The critical concern is moisture sealing the OSB core — not alkalinity. Tannin bleed is not a significant concern for engineered wood (zinc borate treatment and MDI resin suppress extractive bleed).

exterior_substrate_states.description: Engineered wood with field-applied exterior primer — ready for topcoat.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Light dust-off. Minimal prep — surface is paint-ready.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Assumes proper exterior primer was applied. Direct topcoat application. This state occurs when prime and finish are split across mobilizations.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Factory-finished engineered wood (LP SmartSide ExpertFinish or equivalent). Multi-coat factory finish compromised by construction activity, caulking, handling damage, or general construction wear.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Low-pressure wash. Light scuff sand entire surface for adhesion profile. Clean caulk residue and construction debris.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Bonding primer — the factory baked finish is a non-standard substrate for field paint adhesion. Bonding primer ensures mechanical grip on the cured factory topcoat.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Common NC scenario. ExpertFinish siding arrives finished but after installation, caulking, and construction traffic the finish is no longer acceptable. Field prime with bonding primer + 2 topcoats restores appearance. The factory finish warranty is effectively void once field painting is performed.

exterior_access_type_analysis.treatment: Modifier on tasks, not a site condition. Same concept as FAC_HEIGHT for interior.

scenarios.notes: Single-story siding, first 8 ft. No ladder needed. Baseline rate.
Two-story siding, gable ends, areas above 8 ft. Constant repositioning. Safety overhead.
Large continuous areas above 8 ft. Setup/teardown amortized. Better than ladder for runs >50 LF.
Boom/scissor lift for 3+ story or difficult access. Requires firm ground. Rental cost.

exterior_environmental_constraints.note: Environmental constraints are documented here for SOP reference but are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers per RC-003 correction from wood siding spec.

sop_reference_only.note: Below 50F: slow cure, adhesion risk. Above 85F: flash dry, blistering on dark colors.

sop_reference_only.rule: Surface temp must be >= 5 deg F above dew point
sop_reference_only.note: Adhesion and blushing risk at marginal conditions.

sop_reference_only.rule: Engineered wood: < 15% MC before painting. More moisture-retentive at joints and cut ends than fiber cement.
sop_reference_only.note: OSB core retains moisture longer than cementitious substrates.

production_rate_research.source: Exterior_Application_Methods_Doctrine.md, Exterior_Engineered_Wood_Fiber_Cement_Doctrine.md, calibrated against sibling specs SF_SIDING_FIBERCEMENT_EXT_NC_v1 and SF_WOOD_SIDING_EXT_NC_PAINT_v1

lap_spray.notes: Airless spray, smooth LP SmartSide lap. 517 tip. Higher end for long uninterrupted runs. ~10-15% faster than fiber cement lap due to lighter weight and faster handling.

lap_spray_backroll.notes: Spray + back-roll on textured (cedarmill/roughsawn) lap profiles. 2-person crew. Rate reduction from pure spray due to back-roll pass.

lap_brush_roll.notes: Brush for edges/transitions, roller for field. Fallback method. Slightly faster than fiber cement brush/roll (lighter boards).

t1_11_spray_backroll.notes: Mandatory spray + back-roll for T1-11 groove profile. Deep grooves require roller to distribute paint. 2-person crew.

t1_11_brush_roll.notes: Brush for grooves, roller for field panels. Labor-intensive but no spray setup.

panel_spray.notes: Large flat panels, fewer joints than lap. 517 tip. Fast runs on uninterrupted panel surfaces.

panel_brush_roll.notes: Roller for field, brush at panel joints and edges.

field_prime_spray.notes: Spray primer on factory-primed engineered wood. Straightforward — good adhesion base. Slightly faster than fiber cement due to non-alkaline surface.

end_seal.notes: Brush sealant on cut ends. Critical task — cannot be skipped.

low_pressure_wash.notes: Garden hose + soft brush. Faster than pressure wash because lower setup.

caulk_siding_joints.notes: Siding-to-trim joint caulking. Gun + finger tool. Do NOT caulk butt joints.

key_decisions.decision: Combined (full phase_scope). Prime and finish phases have unique task keys within the single spec.
key_decisions.rationale: NC engineered wood siding is a single-mobilization scope — same crew primes and paints. Each phase (prime, finish) has its own task IDs and module IDs for independent rate tracking and phase-level reporting. Matches fiber cement and wood siding sibling spec pattern.

key_decisions.decision: Include siding_profile dimension: lap, panel, t1_11
key_decisions.rationale: Production rates vary significantly by profile (lap spray 300+ SF/hr vs T1-11 spray+backroll 150-200 SF/hr). Profile affects application method constraints — T1-11 mandates spray_backroll.

key_decisions.topic: Back-rolling policy — KEY DIFFERENCE from fiber cement
key_decisions.decision: Back-rolling is MANDATORY on T1-11 and textured profiles, OPTIONAL on smooth LP SmartSide lap.
key_decisions.rationale: Per Exterior_Application_Methods_Doctrine Part A §6: 'T-1-11 and rough-sawn siding: Deep vertical grooves need roller to distribute paint.' This is the OPPOSITE of fiber cement (which avoids back-rolling to preserve factory-smooth surface).

key_decisions.topic: Substrate state scope — uses SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD not SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT
key_decisions.decision: Four NC-relevant states: SS_EXT_PRIMED_FACTORY, SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD, SS_EXT_PRIMED_FIELD, SS_EXT_FACTORY_FINISHED. Repaint states excluded.
key_decisions.rationale: This is a new construction spec. Engineered wood is wood-based, not cementitious — uses SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD for bare surfaces. Factory-finished (ExpertFinish) included because post-construction damage commonly requires field painting. The researcher prompt incorrectly listed SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT — corrected in RC-001.

key_decisions.topic: Surface texture as modifier vs dimension
key_decisions.decision: Surface texture (smooth, cedarmill, roughsawn) is a MODIFIER on production and material, not a configuration dimension.
key_decisions.rationale: Texture affects rate and material quantity (surface_factor 1.15-1.30) but does not change the task structure or module sequence. It is a multiplier, not a workflow branch. Note: T1-11 groove pattern IS part of the siding_profile dimension because it changes application method constraints.

key_decisions.decision: NOT this spec's responsibility. Per sibling spec RC-001.
key_decisions.rationale: Window/door protection belongs in window/door specs. Prevents double-counting. Clear ownership per surface.

key_decisions.decision: EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers. Per sibling spec RC-003.
key_decisions.rationale: Environmental conditions are unpredictable at bid time. They are SOP/process concerns documented for field reference but not included in production rate modifiers.

key_decisions.decision: Treated as a HEIGHT MODIFIER, not a site condition. Per sibling spec RC-004.
key_decisions.rationale: Access type drives a rate multiplier on tasks at elevation — conceptually identical to FAC_HEIGHT for interior.

key_decisions.decision: 1 field prime + 2 finish coats standard at all tiers for NC.
key_decisions.rationale: LP SmartSide warranty requires field prime + minimum 2 topcoats from LP-approved paint system. QT2 may accept single finish coat on field-primed surfaces per Exterior_Substrates_Doctrine §4.5.

key_decisions.decision: Factory-finished products (ExpertFinish) are IN SCOPE as substrate state SS_EXT_FACTORY_FINISHED.
key_decisions.rationale: Post-construction damage, caulking, handling, and general construction activity commonly compromise the factory finish to the point where field painting is required. Requires bonding primer (factory baked finish is non-standard substrate for field paint adhesion) + standard topcoat system.

key_decisions.topic: Primer type — standard acrylic NOT alkali-resistant
key_decisions.decision: Field primer for engineered wood is standard 100% acrylic exterior primer. Do NOT use alkali-resistant primer.
key_decisions.rationale: Engineered wood is an organic wood-fiber product, not cementitious. It has neutral to slightly acidic pH. Alkali-resistant primer (needed for fiber cement pH 13.0) is unnecessary and would be a wasted material upgrade. This is a KEY DIFFERENCE from fiber cement.

research_corrections.original_claim: Researcher prompt listed SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT as a valid substrate state for engineered wood siding
research_corrections.corrected_to: SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT is a fiber cement-specific state. Engineered wood is wood-based and uses SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD for bare/damaged surfaces. Per Substrate_State_Reference.md §4.1: SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD covers 'Raw uncoated wood — no primer, no stain, no finish' which applies to bare engineered wood surfaces. The Exterior_Substrates_Doctrine §2.3 also incorrectly maps engineered wood bare areas to SS_EXT_BARE_FIBERCEMENT — both the prompt and doctrine need correction.

research_corrections.original_claim: Researcher prompt stated 'edge sealing at cut ends' without distinguishing the failure mechanism from fiber cement
research_corrections.corrected_to: Edge sealing on engineered wood prevents moisture intrusion into the OSB core which causes irreversible thickness swell ('springback') due to MDI resin bond failure. This is structurally distinct from fiber cement edge wicking which is cellulose capillary absorption causing edge swelling. The engineered wood failure is more severe — the dimensional change is permanent and cannot be repaired.

research_corrections.original_claim: Researcher prompt stated '22% faster install rate' applies to coating production rates
research_corrections.corrected_to: The 22% faster rate is for siding INSTALLATION (handling, cutting, nailing) due to lighter weight and longer lengths. It does NOT directly translate to 22% faster coating production. Spray/roll rates are determined by surface area and profile geometry, not board weight. However, lighter boards do contribute to marginally faster production when repositioning ladders, scaffolding, and equipment — estimated ~10-15% faster effective production rate than fiber cement for comparable profiles.
